newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African hit-squad boss freed on apartheid murder.
newsitem.headline: S.African hit-squad boss freed on apartheid murder.

text.p: South Africa's High Court halted on Friday the murder trial of notorious hit-squad leader Dirk Coetzee and two of his colleagues following their pardon by the country's truth commission.

Coetzee, a former commander of a clandestine police unit near Pretoria, and police operatives Almond Nofomela and David Tshikalanga, were granted amnesty on Monday for murdering human rights lawyer Griffiths Mxenge in 1981.

"With amnesty having been granted to you, the proceedings against you are terminated. You may step down," Judge Piet Combrinck told the three men in the Indian Ocean port city of Durban where Mxenge was brutally stabbed to death.
A joking and smiling Coetzee told reporters that he finally felt free.
"I am smiling all the way. I am extremely happy. It is the first time in eight years that I have felt truly free," he said.
But he lashed out at Mxenge's brothers for refusing to forgive him, and criticised them for not helping to promote post-apartheid South Africa's drive toward reconciliation.
"I've never seen them (the brothers) smiling and the like. Their faces show revenge and hatred," he told state television.

Coetzee said he felt great sympathy and remorse towards the children of the victim. "But for the brothers, I'm really getting fed up with their nagging and not falling in with the new South Africa," he said.
No comment was immediately available from the Mxenge family on Coetzee's remarks.

A lawyer acting on behalf of the Mxenge family said after the case was withdrawn that an appeal would be made to a higher court for a review of the amnesty decision by the Truth and Reconconciliation Commission (TRC).
"We will be taking the TRC to a high court to review the decision and say if whether the procedure was fair or not," lawyer Imraan Moosa told Reuters.

Coetzee defected to President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress (ANC) after blowing the whistle in 1989 on the clandestine "Vlakplaas" police unit he headed as well as a series of murders carried out by the unit's covert hit-squads in the fight against the ANC.
Coetzee, who was the target of a failed assassination attempt by his former colleagues after he defected, now works for the post-apartheid government's espionage service.
He said on Friday he was suspended from service pending the outcome of the trial and could not say if he would return to his job.

"I was the guy who blew the cover on the hit-squads and lost everything. I feel someone owes me something and only the ANC can provide that," Coetzee told Reuters. "If they look after me and give me a proper position, I'll remain loyal to them."
Coetzee, Nofomela and Tshikalanga were given amnesty by the truth commission earlier this week on the grounds that they had been acting on the orders of senior officers.
However, they still have a long list of crimes for which they are seeking amnesty. Nofomela, a former police sergeant, is in jail serving a life term for an unrelated murder.
